text: Ivan Petrov / Age: 26
Rank/Position: Red Army soldier (private), rifleman
Civilian Occupation: History teacher
Origin: Voronezh city / surrounding area, RSFSR
Ivan Petrov was driven by one thing only: patriotism in its purest form. His heart beat
for the nation and the motherland.
It was almost religious, and he was certain that this devotion, this worship of home,
was what kept him alive.
Doctors told his parents early on that he was a sick, fragile boy, not built for this
world.
“Protect him from everything,” the doctor said.
“Even from the wind. There's no medicine I can prescribe for what he has.”
His parents listened.
They kept him wrapped in comfort.
They treated him like porcelain.
And Ivan hated it.
He begged for the same rough, ordinary life his siblings got.
The same life other boys got.
They wouldn't even let him work summers to earn a little money.
They wouldn't let him play outside in daylight.
He was allowed out only at dusk, when the sun couldn't burn him.
He couldn't even leave the street, so his mother could observe him from the kitchen window.
The other children made it even worse.
They pushed him out.
They didn't want him on their team.
Whether they were kicking the ball or playing war, it was always the same.
If Ivan was on your side, you were at a disadvantage.
After a while, he stopped
asking to go out. He stayed in his room instead. He liked the half-dark that the lowered blinds
created. He put on his thick-framed glasses, glasses he would never wear in front of the
other boys if he could help it, and squinted his way through book after book from his father's
inexhaustible library. It didn't take long for him to convince himself
that it was better to read about the injustices done to his homeland during the Napoleonic wars
than to choke in the dust outside. That Lenin's immortal ideas could soothe an ordinary Russian
youth even when his chest began to sting like an old man's. In time, Ivan formed a belief
as solid as iron. Russia had been robbed of its greatness again and again,
or at least, the West had tried to rob it.
It didn't matter though,
which conquerors came to defile the holy soil.
In the end, they always failed.
That belief is why he became a history teacher.
So he could pass the idea of national greatness
into as many unpolished minds as possible.
In his modest way,
he would help ensure that
the motherland remained in good hands in the generations to come. But daytime speeches
in a classroom didn't fully satisfy his hunger for justice, so in the evenings he went to
pubs and cafés. He never drank a drop of alcohol, and yet he behaved like a drunk. Flushed
face, bright eyes, climbing onto chairs, onto tables,
sometimes straight onto the counter, preaching what should be done to the nations that threatened
Mother Russia. Naturally, when the motherland needed him most, there was never any question
of whether he would go to war. He knew there were cowardly traitors who would gladly hide behind
a weak body, men who would fold their hands in gratitude if poor health excused them from service.
Ivan was not one of them.
On the contrary, he reached into his pocket
and used a significant portion of the money
he'd inherited from his parents to grease the right palms,
to persuade the decision-making doctors
to look away from his irregular heartbeat,
to ignore the lungs that worked at 70 percent capacity.
And now he leans out of the trench and fires.
He keeps firing.
And he sings at the top of his lungs — The Sacred War.
He's the most surprised of all that his voice doesn't crack,
that his breathing doesn't whistle.
The sound comes out clean and clear into the frozen air,
as if the cold can't touch him.
As if bullets fired by men who fight without conviction can't touch him either.
And if death does catch him here, Ivan isn't afraid.
He only hopes the sun will come out.
That the thick crust of ice over the ground will finally soften,
so that the sweet motherland, his mother earth, can drink, to the last drop,
the blood of her fragile child.
